stories.title: First-line dolutegravir/lamivudine in HIV-1 infection: lymph node penetration and reservoir decline in a randomized open-label clinical trial
stories.description: Dual antiretroviral therapy with dolutegravir and lamivudine (DTG/3TC) is a recommended first-line regimen for people with HIV, but whether reduced-drug therapy maintains adequate antiviral pressure within lymph node (LN) reservoirs remains uncertain. In the DUALITY clinical trial (EudraCT number 2019-002733-10), the prespecified primary endpoint—change in proviral HIV-1 DNA in peripheral blood CD4 + T cells from baseline to week 48—was similar between participants initiating DTG/3TC or dolutegravir-based triple therapy. Here, we investigated prespecified secondary endpoints comprising viral persistence and antiretroviral drug penetration and distribution in LN using multimodal imaging. In 39 participants undergoing inguinal LN excision at baseline or during the first year of treatment, HIV-1 DNA and RNA were detected by DNAscope/RNAscope and antiretroviral spatial distribution was mapped by mass spectrometry imaging. HIV-1–infected cells declined rapidly after treatment initiation across both treatment groups. Antiretrovirals were widely detected within LN tissue regions containing or adjacent to HIV-positive cells. These findings provide spatial evidence that DTG/3TC reaches LN tissue and HIV-positive cells, extending peripheral blood observations to a key anatomical HIV reservoir. In this study, Jose Molto and colleagues report data from a randomised open-label clinical trial showing of first-line dolutegravir/lamivudine treatment for HIV-1. They report that the treatment reaches lymph nodes and regions containing HIV-positive cells, which strengthens evidence for antiviral exposure within a key anatomical HIV reservoir.

stories.title: Switchable quantum dot photoluminescence across a broad spectrum with all-visible-light activated diarylethene photoswitches
stories.description: Precise and reversible photoluminescence switching is highly attractive for optical memory, bioimaging, and smart displays. However, achieving broadband photoluminescence modulation through a simple and general strategy remains challenging, while the ultraviolet light requirement of most molecular photoswitches limits practical applications. Here, we achieve all-visible-light activated reversible photoluminescence modulation of quantum dots across an ultrawide spectral range of nearly 500 nm from blue to near-infrared region using diarylethene photoswitches. In the ring-open form of diarylethenes, quantum dots emitting blue, green, red, white and near-infrared light remain in the photoluminescence on-state. Under 405 nm irradiation, diarylethenes undergo ring-closure through triplet sensitization by CdS quantum dots, resulting in significant photoluminescence quenching to the off-state, with the maximum efficiency of 99.6% and an on/off ratio up to 250. Green-light irradiation reverses the diarylethenes back to the ring-open form, fully restoring the photoluminescence on-state. Our approach further enables reversible multi-level data storage and near-infrared anti-counterfeiting, highlighting the potential for smart light-responsive materials and optoelectronic devices. Achieving photoswitchable luminescence across a broad wavelength range remains challenging. Here, the authors integrate diarylethene photoswitches with quantum dots, enabling visible-light on-off switching of photoluminescence from blue to near-infrared across nearly 500 nm range, with applications in data storage and anti-counterfeiting.
